title: Asha the Alpaca's Wonderful Wobbly Chairs
markdown:
Beside a babbling brook lived Asha, an alpaca as fluffy as a well-kept cloud and as particular as a ruler. She wore spectacles and believed everything must be just so. One misplaced strand of fleece could, in her view, unravel the afternoon.

Every day she practised her poem for the Whispering Willow Poetry Recital. She stood before her reflection, polishing her fleece until it behaved. The spectacles slid; she nudged them back; her brow knitted. The recital hall — a cozy hollow under an ancient willow — was her haven of perfect order, chairs in rows that could have passed an inspection.

Young Benji, a bear cub with paws like dinner plates, prepared too. His talent was booming cub roars that made leaves consider other careers. He was a whirl of good intentions and elbows. Old Mr. Lake, who lived by the shimmering water and hummed as if the lake had asked him to, watched them both with a knowing smile and a walking stick that wore a small bell.

One blustery afternoon the wind tumbled into the hall and treated the chairs as a suggestion. Asha’s precise rows became a delightful disarray: some tumbled, some tipped, one appeared to be consulting the ceiling.

Asha’s fluffy heart fluttered. Spectacles misted. “This simply will not do. The symmetry is broken.” She began measuring the distance between each chair with a careful hoof, twenty-two and a half inches, because half an inch was how a day came apart.

Benji bounded in. “I can help!” He tried to nudge a chair. His paw sent it skittering. It bumped another, then another, a charmingly chaotic pattern that would have made a surveyor sit down. Asha let out a tiny distressed bleat.

Mr. Lake cleared his throat. “Remarkable, Benji. A whole forest of chairs.”

The stage looked like furniture having a chat. One chair leaned companionably. Another seemed to be doing a jig. A third sat off to the side, contemplating the rafters. Asha’s panic, after a long argument with itself, began to melt. The chairs were not only misplaced. They had opinions. Benji giggled, a deep rumble that the willow took as applause.

The wind gave a gentler sigh. Leaves rustled overhead. Benji, forgetting haste, peered at the arrangement with actual interest. Mr. Lake chuckled, and the stick’s bell tinkled as if it had been waiting for permission. He did not ask the willow what else it knew. He only said, “Wind and tumbled chairs. A surprise with legs.”

Asha picked up the last chair. She did not measure. She did not fret. She set it with a gentle thump at a slight charming angle, the sort of angle a poem might use if a poem had furniture. The hall, instead of feeling disrupted, felt awake. The chairs seemed to nod. Quiet laughter moved between alpaca, cub, and old gentleman like a shared blanket.

Ever since, the Whispering Willow Poetry Recital has been talked about for its wobbly chairs, and Asha has practised her poem standing slightly off-centre on purpose. She logged twenty-two-and-a-half / Benji-skitter / last chair at an angle in the recital book, left the measuring string in her fleece-bag unused, and let Benji roar once for luck at a chair that was already leaning. The brook, which had been babbling the whole time, did not correct anyone.
